name: Open Container Initiative (OCI) specifications
vendor: Open Container Initiative (Linux Foundation), founded by Docker, CoreOS and others

foundation.via: Published by the Open Container Initiative, an LF project run by its own Technical Oversight Board

summary: Three vendor-neutral standards that let any build tool, registry and runtime share containers: how a runtime starts one, how an image is laid out, and the HTTP API registries use to push and pull it.
intro: The Open Container Initiative maintains three specifications. The Runtime Specification starts from a filesystem bundle, a directory holding a root filesystem and a `config.json` that sets the process, mounts, namespaces, cgroups and other limits, and defines the operations every runtime must offer: `create`, `start`, `kill`, `delete` and `state`, with hooks at fixed points in between. It covers Linux, Windows, Solaris, z/OS and, since version 1.3 in November 2025, FreeBSD, plus a `vm` section for runtimes that start a virtual machine. The Image Specification describes what a builder produces: an image index lists one manifest per platform, and each manifest points to a configuration (environment, entry point, layer order) and a list of layers, tar archives of filesystem changes. Each reference is a descriptor carrying a media type, a size and a digest, so every piece is named by its hash and verified on arrival. The Distribution Specification, based on Docker’s Registry HTTP API V2, defines the `/v2/` endpoints for pulling manifests and blobs by tag or digest, uploading blobs then manifests, listing tags, deleting, and mounting a blob from another repository.

Because the formats are shared, the pieces are interchangeable: an image built by Docker or Podman can be stored in Harbor, Quay or a cloud registry and started by runc, crun, youki, gVisor’s `runsc` or Kata Containers, all listed as runtime-spec implementations. Version 1.1 of the image and distribution specs, in February 2024, made registries general content stores. Any file can be pushed as an artifact, an ordinary image manifest with an `artifactType` field, and a `subject` field points one manifest at another, so a signature, SBOM or attestation can be attached to an image. The new referrers API (`GET /v2/<name>/referrers/<digest>`) lists what points at an image. The OCI also hosts runc, the reference runtime. A Technical Oversight Board, in 2026 with members from Microsoft, IBM, Docker, AWS, Google and others, settles cross-project issues and decides which projects the OCI takes on.
strengths: Build, store and run are decoupled: any conforming builder, registry and runtime work together, so switching one doesn’t mean rebuilding images
Everything is content-addressed: a digest names exact bytes, so pulls are verifiable and identical layers are stored and transferred once
Registries carry more than images: since 1.1, Helm charts, signatures, SBOMs and other artifacts sit next to the image they describe, found through the referrers API
Vendor-neutral: maintained in the open under the Linux Foundation, overseen by a board drawn from competing companies
limits: They cover formats and interfaces only: how an image is built (a Dockerfile, for example), how containers are networked and how they are orchestrated are outside the OCI’s scope
Referrers support is uneven: clients must fall back to a tag scheme (`sha256-<digest>`) on older registries, which the OCI notes is open to race conditions and clutters tag lists
Slow, consensus-driven change: the image spec went from 1.0 in July 2017 to 1.1 in February 2024, and a dedicated artifact manifest was dropped before 1.1 over portability concerns
Docker’s heritage still shows: the distribution spec warns clients may meet Docker-specific headers and error codes, and older Docker manifest media types remain in use

sections.title: A signature attached to an image
sections.intro: Since 1.1 an artifact is an image manifest with an `artifactType`. With no configuration to carry, it points at the standard two-byte empty descriptor (`{}`), and `subject` ties it to the image it signs. A registry returns it from `GET /v2/<name>/referrers/<image digest>`. Illustrative values.

story: By 2015 Docker’s image format and runtime had become the de facto way to package software, and the company controlled both. CoreOS had answered with its own runtime, rkt, and an alternative image spec, appc, and the rift worried companies building on containers. On June 22, 2015, at DockerCon in San Francisco, Docker, CoreOS and others announced the Open Container Project under the Linux Foundation; the founding members included AWS, Google, IBM, Intel, Microsoft, Red Hat and VMware. Docker donated its container format and its runtime, runC, as the starting point, and appc’s maintainers joined in.

Runtime Specification 1.0 and Image Format Specification 1.0 were released on July 19, 2017. The image format took ideas from both appc and Docker’s v2.2 image format, while signing and the transport of images over an API were left for later. The Distribution Specification, based on Docker’s Registry HTTP API V2, reached 1.0 on May 5, 2021.

Supply-chain security drove the next change. Signatures and SBOMs needed a home next to the images they describe, and tools had been storing them under special tag names. Image and Distribution 1.1, released on February 15, 2024, added artifacts, the `subject` field and the referrers API. Runtime 1.3 followed in November 2025, adding FreeBSD as a platform.

choices.choice: Start from Docker’s code and formats
choices.why: A standard that broke existing images would not have been adopted. Docker donated its runtime and format, and the image format was designed to stay compatible with Docker’s and appc’s, so existing tools could adopt it.

choices.choice: Name every piece by its digest
choices.why: Manifests, configurations and layers are referenced by descriptors carrying a hash, so a client can check what it downloaded, identical layers are shared, and an image reference by digest can never change underneath you.

choices.choice: Reuse the image manifest for artifacts
choices.why: The 1.1 release candidates had a separate artifact manifest, but it was removed because registries and clients that only understood image manifests could not store or copy it. An image manifest with an `artifactType` works with existing registries.
